h: Governments that tame the media end up blind
dek: In The Wire, Omair Ahmad writes that governments which tighten their grip on the media end up cut off from the reality of their own country, and the US midterms and India's current protests show it.
body: Omair Ahmad, who has worked as a political analyst and journalist in India, the US and Britain, makes a simple argument: a government that gets the media in its fist looks like it is winning for a while, but slowly it loses any sense of what is really happening in the country. His latest example is the US midterm elections. From The New York Times to Fox News, outlets called certain candidates 'too extreme' for backing trans rights or public healthcare for all, and most of those candidates won comfortably.

According to the writer, Bari Weiss, the new head at CBS, pushed to link Abdul El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, but El-Sayed won too. Meanwhile the channel lost viewers: the September 2026 season opening of '60 Minutes' was watched by 21 per cent fewer people than in 2025. The debate on X also steered the Republican Party in the wrong direction, while little Bluesky and local non-profit outlets such as Mississippi Free Press and Bolts were closer to the reality on the ground.

To get to the root of this sickness, Ahmad recalls British journalist Nick Davies's 2008 book 'Flat Earth News'. Davies examined about 2,000 articles from four major newspapers over two weeks and found that only 12 per cent of the content came from the papers' own reporters. Most of the rest came from PR agencies and wire services. The causes were ownership concentrated in a few hands, small bureaus shutting down and the pressure to publish fast.

Then the piece turns to ownership. In the US, the Ellison family holds CBS, CNN, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, and got relief on mergers from the Trump administration. In India, the Ambani group dominates everything from entertainment to TV. Elon Musk gave Republican campaigns about $500 million, said to be the biggest election donation ever by a single person, and still the party could not sense the public's anger.

On India, the writer says the government looked shaky after the 2024 results in Uttar Pradesh, and there is a straight line from that period to today's protests, which it cannot manage by controlling the narrative. His conclusion is that elections and protests are only the first step; until the monopoly structure of the media changes, the restoration of democracy will stay incomplete.
nazar: This piece is a reminder that press freedom is not only a journalists' issue; it is about whether those in power can see and hear at all. When the big channels are in the hands of one or two business houses and small, grassroots outlets are pushed down, the first news to vanish is about workers, farmers, Dalits and minorities, because reaching them takes effort and they do not bring advertising.
Protecting independent digital media, local reporters and the voice of people's movements in India is therefore a basic condition of democracy, not a favour to any one party.
sawal: When 88 per cent of the news is borrowed, how can anyone read the public mood?
ref: Churnalism
A word coined by Nick Davies. The habit of rushing press releases and agency copy into print without any reporting on the ground.
Fourth estate
The idea of the press as the fourth pillar of democracy, whose job is to keep watch on power and tell citizens the truth.
ank: share of British newspaper stories from PR and agencies

h: Deaths at the IITs: why Dalit and Adivasi scholars want institutions of their own
dek: In The India Forum, Jyoti Baniya and Ashok Danavath argue that instead of hoping to reform the existing IITs, India should build separate national institutions for caste-oppressed students.
body: In September, Sahil Wakode, a Dalit student at IIT Bombay, took his own life a few hours after a professor accused him of cheating. According to the writers, the charge was never proven, the institute's set procedure for exam cases was not followed, and an invigilator had threatened to 'ruin' his career. The same institute also saw the deaths of Aniket Ambhore in 2014 and Darshan Solanki in 2025.

Jyoti Baniya, a Dalit scholar from Assam, and Ashok Danavath, an Adivasi (indigenous) scholar, lay out the numbers. Of the 45 students who died by suicide at the IITs between 2020 and 2025, 62 per cent were SC, ST or OBC, while reservation for these groups is 49.5 per cent. Between 2019 and 2023, 8,139 students from these groups dropped out. Of the 6,043 teachers at 23 IITs, Dalits are only 2.5 per cent, and Adivasis number just 21.

The writers say that after the death, alumni and faculty forums, which they describe as almost entirely upper caste, were seen standing with the accused professor, while very little was done on the inquiry or the question of discrimination. So instead of reform, they talk of an alternative: separate IITs for caste-oppressed students, run by Dalit and Adivasi scholars and administrators.

For this they point to the historically Black colleges of the US and the tribal colleges set up there since 1968. In India they mention Ambedkar's People's Education Society, founded in 1945, the proposed Dalit university in Telangana, Aligarh, Jamia and the women's universities. Citing Paulo Freire, they say that in such institutions these students will not be objects of research but creators of knowledge.

The writers accept that separate institutions will not end discrimination in the mainstream, but they ask how long caste-oppressed students must keep swallowing humiliation while sitting the test of 'merit'.
nazar: This proposal will make many people uncomfortable, and it should. When the deaths and dropouts of Dalit and Adivasi students at the country's most famous institutions are on record, and reserved teaching posts have stayed unfilled for years, the demand for separate institutions is really a statement of no confidence in the present system.

The real answer would be for the IITs themselves to tighten their anti-discrimination systems, fill the empty reserved posts and hold an independent inquiry into every death; only then will the Constitution's promise of equality reach the campus.
sawal: Only 21 Adivasi teachers across 23 IITs: is that merit, or a closed door?
ref: Historically Black colleges (HBCU)
Colleges set up in the US for Black students during the era of racial segregation, which kept running after segregation ended.
People's Education Society
The body Dr Ambedkar founded in 1945, which opened Siddharth College in Mumbai and Milind College in Aurangabad.

h: Karnataka must not waste its chance to heal the wounds of SIR
dek: A Deccan Herald editorial says the Special Summary Revision is a chance to correct the mistakes of SIR, as long as it does not become another purge.
body: The Election Commission has ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) in the states where SIR has been completed. According to the Deccan Herald editorial, this is a chance to make up for the damage SIR did. In Karnataka, after SIR, the number of voters fell from 5.54 crore to 4.55 crore (55.4 million to 45.5 million), which means more than 99 lakh (9.9 million) names were cut. The final roll is due on 20 January 2027.

The paper points out that the Commission has now made clear that voters do not need to link themselves to the 2002 roll. The editorial reads this as an admission that SIR put an unfair burden on people and was badly planned. But for West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Bihar, where SIR came right before elections, this correction came far too late. In Bengal, about 21 lakh appeals were still pending months after the polls ended.

The editorial does not spare the political parties either. The Congress abandoned its early campaign midway, when documenting even a hundred clear cases could have changed the debate. The BJP faces charges of targeting minority voters. The Karnataka High Court has stayed the investigation of FIRs against BJP booth agents accused of filing Form 7 in bulk. The Commission itself admits to more than 91,000 Form 7s, but says no name was cut on their basis.

A month after Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar's sit-in at the office of the Chief Electoral Officer, there has been no concrete action on false claims of death and change of address, which the paper sees as raising questions about the Commission's neutrality. Its demand is that no name be removed without an inquiry into bulk objections, a hearing and written reasons, and that parties use their booth agents to get every eligible voter's name added back.
nazar: 99 lakh names equal the population of a whole state. The weight of such a purge falls hardest on migrant workers, the poor, minorities and people with weak paperwork, who cannot run around filing appeals.

The right to vote is protected by adding names, not cutting them. If false objections go unpunished in the SSR as well, people's trust that the Election Commission belongs equally to every citizen will break further.
sawal: Who has yet asked for answers from those who filed 91,000 Form 7s?
ref: Form 7
The form for objecting to a name on the voter roll and seeking its removal. Any voter can object to someone else's name.
Special Summary Revision
The yearly or regular revision of the voter roll, in which new names are added and errors corrected; it is a lighter process than SIR.

h: Draw the map of a new province first, hold the referendum later
dek: In Dawn, Pakistan's former attorney general Ashtar Ausaf Ali writes that asking the public yes or no on a proposal whose shape has not even been decided is doing things backwards.
body: In Pakistan, the debate on creating new provinces has become a source of strain within the ruling coalition. The interior minister spoke of a referendum on it, and the information minister held a press conference. Former attorney general Ashtar Ausaf Ali says people are being asked to put their stamp on an idea whose outline nobody has seen.

He asks what a new province would change for an ordinary citizen: where land disputes will be settled, who will collect taxes, how much it will cost and who will pay. According to the writer, the answers so far differ from province to province.

He spells out the constitutional route clearly. Under Article 239, changing a province's boundary needs a two-thirds majority in both houses of parliament, as well as a two-thirds majority in the assembly of the affected province. The writer calls this the constitutional veto of the people affected. A referendum can be held under Article 48, but in his view its result cannot replace these majorities, and a nationwide vote could impose a change whose price is paid by a single province.

Ali wants the process to begin with grievances: how long it takes to reach a hospital or an office, and how much development money went where. Every proposal should come with an administrative map, financial estimates for five and ten years, and the division of courts, water, gas, mineral revenue, debt and pensions. It should also explain how a new province would achieve what cannot be done by giving power to local governments under Article 140A.
His suggestion is an independent commission that makes its evidence public and holds hearings in every affected area, including remote districts and minority communities.
nazar: India has seen maps redrawn from Telangana to Jammu and Kashmir, and in Jammu and Kashmir the assembly was not even asked. Ali's point applies to both countries: before a boundary line is drawn, the people whose lives it will change must be heard, especially those who live far from the capital.
sawal: How will the voices of remote districts be counted in a referendum?
ref: Article 239

The provision in Pakistan's Constitution that sets out how it is amended.
Changing a province's boundary also needs two-thirds consent of that province's assembly.
Article 140A

Places on Pakistan's provinces the duty to set up local governments.
Under it, political, administrative and financial powers are to be handed down to the lowest level.

h: Sudan's war will end through exhaustion, not diplomacy
dek: In Al Jazeera, Cameron Hudson writes that a collapsing currency, empty fields and the pressure of returning people are pushing Sudan towards a ceasefire; the only question is whether it will come in time.
body: Sudan's war is in its fourth year, and from the outside there is no end in sight. The US is piling sanctions on sanctions to make the fighting costly and bring both sides to the negotiating table. Cameron Hudson argues that international diplomacy has failed and that the pressure for a ceasefire is now building from inside the country.

Back from a few days in Khartoum in November, the writer says flights from Cairo, Riyadh and Doha are landing regularly at the airport, returning people are putting their lives back together, and foreign businesspeople are hunting for mining and reconstruction deals. But the Sudanese pound, at 600 to the dollar before the war, has now crossed 10,000.

Of the roughly 3.8 million people who fled the country, more than 2 million have come back and are struggling with the cost of food, electricity and water. Farmers cannot afford fertiliser, so the most fertile land lies fallow. According to the writer, a senior official admitted to him privately that the war economy that paid for the weapons is now the biggest source of pain. Protests over rent are rising in Atbara, the same city where the 2018 bread protests began.

On the front lines, the army holds nearly two-thirds of the country, while Darfur is almost entirely in the hands of the RSF. During the RSF's capture of El Fasher a year ago, the atrocities committed showed signs of genocide to a UN fact-finding mission.

More than 40 per cent of the population faces severe food insecurity, and this year's 'super El Nino' has upset the rains. Hudson says only a ceasefire in the coming months can open the way for relief on a large scale.
nazar: The world's biggest displacement crisis meets silence in India's news, even though we have an old bond with Sudan. Hudson's account holds a lesson: wars often stop when ordinary people's plates are empty, and by then women, children and farmers have already paid the heaviest price.
sawal: Who will put bread on the table for the two million Sudanese who have come home?
ref: RSF

Rapid Support Forces, Sudan's paramilitary force led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, 'Hemedti'.
Since April 2023 it has been fighting the army of military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan.
Atbara

A railway city in northern Sudan with a history of workers' movements.
In December 2018, protests over the price of bread began here, leading to the fall of Omar al-Bashir in 2019.

h: The Antalya draft: a statement on prohibition that never mentions alcohol
dek: In Common Dreams, Kumi Naidoo writes that the name of fossil fuels has vanished from the final COP31 draft, and that countries still have time to dig in their heels.
body: COP31, the UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkiye, has run past its scheduled end. Kumi Naidoo, former head of Greenpeace International and Amnesty International and now chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, writes from the sidelines of the summit that he feels both grief and disbelief.

According to the writer, every mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the latest draft, and the proposed promise of money for adaptation has been taken out too. He compares this to an anti-addiction group that has been writing statements for thirty years without the word alcohol appearing anywhere, and whose meetings have liquor companies as the biggest delegation.

Naidoo recalls a meeting held not long ago in Santa Marta, Colombia, where governments, movements, scientists, Indigenous communities and people from the hardest-hit regions gathered to talk about moving beyond fossil fuels. Back then it felt as if political will could catch up with the urgency of the science.

He backs Panama, which he says should lodge a formal objection if the final text lacks a promise to end production, concrete climate finance and a guarantee of renewable power. The writer says Nepal too is close to walking out, because rich countries are ignoring the devastation it faces.

Naidoo asks what electrification means without a plan for where the power comes from, and how countries can keep their promises without money. That those who did least to cause the crisis suffer the most is something he does not hesitate to call climate apartheid. His demand is a fast, fair and funded exit.
nazar: From the Himalayas to the Sundarbans, India lies in the same kind of regions Nepal is speaking for. The disappearance of adaptation money from the draft will hit first the farmers, fishers and workers who live through floods and heatwaves. Along with listing its own compulsions over coal, India must decide whether it will stand with its neighbour or with those who stay silent.
sawal: A draft that does not name fossil fuels: whom does it protect?
ref: COP31

The 31st annual summit of the countries in the UN climate agreement.
It is being held in Antalya, Turkiye, in November 2026.
Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty

A proposed agreement modelled on the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Its aim is to stop new production of coal, oil and gas and gradually end existing production.

h: The real fight over inflation is about who controls resources
dek: In Jacobin, Swedish journalist Oscar Brandt writes that the oil shock from the Iran war could again become an excuse for cuts, when inflation is really a fight over power and control of resources.
body: Whenever prices rise, the first finger is pointed at welfare schemes and government spending. Swedish journalist and historian Oscar Brandt argues that inflation is really a fight over control of concrete resources such as wages, energy, raw materials and productive capacity, and also over who bears the burden of higher prices.

He reminds readers that in 2022, profits in the eurozone grew faster than output and made up the largest share of price rises. In fifteen European countries, the market share of the four biggest firms rose from 26 to 32 per cent between 2000 and 2019. According to the writer, a crisis gives big companies cover to raise prices.

Citing the 1973 oil crisis, he says oil companies, banks and arms makers profited then, workers bore the inflation, and governments then used the same crisis to attack welfare and full-employment policies. Brandt sees this not as something that happens on its own but as a political choice.

Today, when the Middle East war stopped ships in the Strait of Hormuz, petrol and diesel in Sweden became 25 per cent dearer. But the government there halved VAT on groceries in April, which cut food prices by 5.5 per cent that month, and from July to December it sold monthly bus and metro passes at half price. The central bank estimates that without these steps, September's inflation would have been double.

On the other side, unemployment is stuck at 8.7 per cent, and support for people long enrolled in job schemes has been cut. Brandt concludes that raising interest rates does not open a sea route, while cheap travel saves money today and cuts dependence on oil tomorrow.
nazar: India imports most of the oil it needs, so every shock in Hormuz reaches kitchens and fares here too. Sweden's experiment shows that a government, if it wants, can lift the burden off ordinary families and share it out. The question here should be why, even in an age of record profits, the poor carry the weight of taxes on petrol and diesel and GST on food.
sawal: When will a Delhi worker get a half-price metro pass?
ref: Strait of Hormuz

The narrow sea route between Iran and Oman.
A large share of the world's seaborne oil trade passes through it.
Disaster capitalism

A term coined by Naomi Klein.
The tendency to use the shock of a crisis to push through policies such as privatisation and welfare cuts.

h: Bhusawal: objections against 14,562 names, only 74 hold up
dek: In Maharashtra's Bhusawal seat, a check of Form 7s filed in bulk found almost every objection baseless, and legal action against the objectors has now begun.
body: During the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter roll in the Bhusawal assembly seat of Maharashtra's Jalgaon district, Form 7s were filed in bulk to get 14,562 people's names removed. Citing a report in The Indian Express, Scroll says that after verification only 74 of these voters were found fit to be removed.

The Congress had complained that 186 people filed piles of objections together. The seat belongs to BJP MLA Sanjay Savkare. After the complaint, 21 objectors withdrew their 2,532 objections on their own. In the remaining cases, notices were sent asking for proof, and booth-level officers checked every application on the spot. All objections except 74 were rejected.

The district administration has now begun legal action against those who, it says, filed objections in bad faith. On 30 October, the Supreme Court had asked the Election Commission to take corrective steps on such forms in Uttar Pradesh. Telangana and Karnataka have also warned of action.

The Supreme Court said in May that the Commission cannot decide anyone's citizenship through the revision. Even so, there have been reports from some states of people cut from the roll having their ration cards blocked and facing hurdles in renewing passports.
nazar: That more than 99 per cent of the objections turned out false shows that Form 7 has become a weapon for cutting names. In Bhusawal the opposition raised the alarm in time, but where nobody keeps watch, poor, migrant and minority voters can quietly drop off the roll. Only when the burden of proof lies on the objector, and false applications are punished in every district, will this stop.
sawal: Who will compensate the 14,488 people targeted by false objections?
ref: Form 7
An application to object to a name on the voter roll or get it removed. Any voter can fill this form against another name in the same area.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission drive in which voters must fill in forms again to prove their eligibility.

h: Bengaluru: deleted names are back, with their old voter ID numbers
dek: At least 1,635 voters removed during SIR have reappeared on the final roll, some in other constituencies, and with the same EPIC number, which goes against the rules.
body: In Bengaluru, at least 1,635 of the voters marked for removal during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) are back on the final voter roll. Citing an investigation by The Hindu, The Wire reports that many of them are now on the roll of a different assembly constituency, but their voter identity card (EPIC) number has not changed.

The Election Commission's rulebook says that if a person removed from the roll re-registers through Form 6, they do not get their old number. Form 6 is meant for new voters. For example, Sudha of Byatarayanapura was shown as dead and removed; she is now on the Anekal roll with the same number.

Such cases were found in 28 assembly constituencies, where people had been put in the categories of absent, shifted, dead or duplicate entry. Most names were cut because enumeration forms were not submitted on time.

On 3 November, the Commission said people left out of the draft roll should re-register through Form 6, which does not keep the old number. On 6 November, it said people wrongly removed in seven states would be restored with their old numbers, but Karnataka was not among them. The question is whether these names survived after verification or whether the process failed.
nazar: If more than one and a half thousand names in a single city came back against the rules, questions about the credibility of the whole revision are bound to arise. Calling living people dead and then quietly adding them somewhere else is a sign not of transparency but of arbitrariness. The Commission should make the record of every such case public.
sawal: Which officer recorded Sudha as dead, and on what basis?
ref: EPIC
Electors Photo Identity Card, that is, the voter ID card. Its number is treated as every voter's permanent identity.
Form 6
The application to register as a new voter. There are separate forms for a change of address or corrections.

h: US commission says Muslims are targeted in SIR, government calls it bias
dek: The Ministry of External Affairs rejected the charges of the US commission on international religious freedom as a political agenda, but the questions on the ground remain.
body: On 20 November, Asif Mahmood, head of the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), alleged that India is targeting Muslim citizens under the cover of the Special Intensive Revision of the voter roll. According to him, Muslims' names are being removed from the roll, they are being called foreigners, and they are being illegally expelled from the country.

Mahmood referred to statements by Home Minister Amit Shah in which Muslims were called infiltrators. On 2 November, Shah had claimed that the three crore (30 million) voters cut in the revision were Bangladeshi infiltrators. On 21 November, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal called the commission biased and said it had an open political agenda.

In its 2026 annual report, the commission has already recommended that India be named a Country of Particular Concern, though its recommendations are not binding. On 14 November, India's ambassador to the US had rebuked the commission over its remarks on Sharjeel Imam.
The opposition alleges that 13 crore voters were deliberately removed in the areas under revision. The Supreme Court has said that citizenship cannot be decided through this process.
nazar: It is easy to brush off foreign criticism as bias, but the answer has to be given in the homes where names were cut and ration cards stopped. When the home minister himself calls the deleted names infiltrators, trust in the fairness of the process weakens. The government could give the most solid answer to the charges by releasing figures of deleted names by religion.
sawal: In which document is the basis for the claim of three crore infiltrators recorded?
ref: USCIRF
An independent commission set up by the US Congress that tracks religious freedom around the world and makes recommendations to the US government.
Country of Particular Concern
A status the US State Department gives to countries with serious violations of religious freedom. Steps such as sanctions become possible after it.

h: Layoffs dressed up as transfers: Bosch to pay each worker Rs 25 lakh
dek: The Bombay High Court held that sending Nashik workers across the country was a ploy to get rid of them, and found the company guilty of unfair labour practice.
body: In a 19 November judgment, the Bombay High Court ordered auto parts maker Bosch Limited to pay Rs 25 lakh to each worker involved in the dispute. The case concerns the 'New Entrant Temporary Workmen' of the Nashik plant, more than 500 of whom had been sent to different parts of the country.

The company argued that stricter emission rules, and Maruti Suzuki and Honda stopping diesel cars, had cut demand for diesel injectors. First it ran a system in which workers could not come on duty when there was no work. The workers won the right to wages for those days too, a ruling that held all the way to the Supreme Court. Then in August 2024 they were called back and, within a few weeks, transferred to distant places. According to the union, 235 workers were dismissed for not going to the new posts.

Justice Sandeep V Marne said the transfers were not for business needs but to get rid of the workers while dodging the legal process for retrenchment. He upheld the Nashik industrial court's finding of unfair labour practice, but set compensation instead of reinstatement. The company had earlier offered 14 lakh and then 18 lakh. If the amount is not paid within six weeks, interest of eight per cent a year will apply.
nazar: This judgment names a trick many companies use: instead of sacking workers outright, send them so far away that they quit on their own. At a time when new labour codes make retrenchment easier, it is important to remember that workers called temporary have rights too. But the lack of reinstatement also shows that even after winning in court, it is hard for a worker to get the job back.
sawal: Where do the 235 workers sent away from Nashik work today?
ref: Unfair labour practice
Acts listed in Maharashtra's MRTU and PULP Act, 1971, that an employer cannot commit against workers or a union, such as a transfer made out of revenge.
Retrenchment process
Under the Industrial Disputes Act, laying off workers requires notice, compensation and, in some cases, government permission.

h: First case under conversion law: a photo in a burqa is not proof
dek: A Mumbai sessions court granted anticipatory bail to a Muslim man accused under Maharashtra's new anti-conversion law, after the young woman told the court the marriage was her own choice.
body: A Mumbai sessions court has granted anticipatory bail on a personal bond of Rs 50,000 to a Muslim man in a case filed under the Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026. Citing Bar and Bench, Siasat reports that this is among the first cases under the new law. The complaint was filed by the mother of a 22-year-old Hindu woman, who alleged that her daughter was made to change her religion on a promise of marriage.

The two were neighbours and grew close during the Covid lockdown. When the father found out in 2022, the family moved from Jogeshwari to Virar. After the father's death, the two began meeting again. In October the woman went to work and did not return. Two days later she told her mother that she had married on 16 October under the Special Marriage Act.

The mother produced an invitation card with a new Muslim name and a photo of her daughter in a burqa. The police told the court no evidence of a nikah (Muslim marriage ceremony) had been found. The woman appeared herself and said she had faced no pressure or inducement. Additional Sessions Judge P A Sane said a name on an invitation or a photo alone does not prove conversion, and given the long relationship between two adults, the elements of Section 3 did not appear to be made out.
nazar: The very first big case under the new law shows how such laws can be used to turn a marriage of choice between two adults into a crime. Here the marriage took place under the Special Marriage Act, which does not require anyone to change religion at all. It is a relief that the court listened to the woman, but not every couple gets the chance or the courage to reach a court.
sawal: Why did a marriage under the Special Marriage Act become a conversion case?
ref: Maharashtra Freedom of Religion Act, 2026
The state's new law that makes conversion by force, fraud or inducement a crime. Its Section 3 bars such conversion.
Special Marriage Act
A 1954 law under which people of different religions can marry without changing their religion.

h: Fossil fuels vanish from new COP31 draft
dek: The revised draft at the Antalya climate summit drops both the call to move away from fossil fuels and the figure of $120 billion for adaptation, which is being seen as a blow to developing countries.
body: On the last day of COP31, the UN climate summit held in Antalya, Turkiye, from 9 to 20 November, the president of the talks, Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen, told Down To Earth that it is not possible to hold warming to 1.5 degrees without electrification. The revised draft of 19 November has shrunk from 18 pages to nine.

The first draft of 16 November had two roadmaps for moving away from fossil fuels; every such mention is gone from the new text. The target of 35 per cent electricity in energy by 2035 survives, but is now voluntary. At COP30 there was a promise to triple adaptation finance by 2035, to at least $120 billion a year; in the new draft, the figure has been replaced by workshops from 2027 to 2030. The language on workers' rights and a just transition has also been loosened.

More than 60 organisations have written an open letter to Bowen. Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign called it a clear retreat, and Meena Raman of Third World Network said developing countries got nothing but workshops. India's environment minister Bhupender Yadav is reported to have opposed the electrification pledge, but was ready to talk if it stayed fully voluntary.
nazar: The climate crisis hits poor countries and their farmers, fishers and workers hardest, and adaptation money was meant for them. Removing the sum and handing out workshops shows that rich countries are once again dodging responsibility. Along with bargaining on electrification, India should stand up as the voice of the Global South on adaptation finance.
sawal: At whose objection was the $120 billion promise cut?
ref: Adaptation finance
The money poor countries need to prepare for climate impacts such as floods, drought and heat, separate from money for cutting emissions.
Just transition
The principle of protecting the livelihoods and rights of workers and communities in coal mines and factories while moving away from fossil fuels.

h: ASHA workers stay put at Freedom Park, turn down chief minister's appeal
dek: ASHA workers on a round-the-clock sit-in in Bengaluru say they will not get up without a written order.
ask: A fixed honorarium of Rs 15,000 a month
body: Karnataka's ASHA workers have been on an indefinite sit-in at Bengaluru's Freedom Park since Tuesday. The protest runs day and night and had still not ended by Saturday.

Their main demand is a fixed monthly honorarium of Rs 15,000. Several long-pending demands come with it. According to reports, the workers have also complained that they have still not been paid for the work they did in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter list and in the state's educational and social survey.

On Saturday, Chief Minister D. K. Shivakumar posted on X asking the workers to end their agitation. He said the government was considering a 'permanent and comprehensive solution' in the coming days, that the demands would be discussed in the cabinet and that the necessary steps would be taken. He called the ASHA workers his sisters and spoke of respecting their service.
But the workers did not back down despite repeated appeals. They say the sit-in will go on until the government issues a concrete official order on their demands.
nazar: ASHA workers carry the load of the government's health schemes in village after village, and then the voter list and survey work is also dumped on them. Calling them 'sisters' is easy; fixing their pay is hard. The workers' insistence on a written order shows how far their trust in spoken promises has worn away.
sawal: Why is the government that had them do the SIR work holding back their pay?
ref: ASHA
Accredited Social Health Activist. They work in villages under the National Health Mission, but are treated as 'volunteers', not employees.
Freedom Park
The place set aside for sit-ins and protests in Bengaluru, which was once the old central jail.

h: Meira Paibi in Imphal's Yurembam demand probe into 'encounter'
dek: Women of the locality demanded a fair inquiry into the death of a former militant killed in an operation by security forces.
ask: A fair inquiry into the security operation and the killing
body: On Saturday, women of Yurembam Awang Leikai in Imphal West district protested against a security operation in which one person was killed and eight were arrested.

According to the police, a joint team of the CRPF and Manipur Police carried out the operation early on 20 November. A cadre of the banned KCP (PWG) was killed and eight people, including the group's chairman, were caught. The police say guns, cartridges and pistols were recovered, and a case has been registered at Patsoi police station.
The dead man has been named as Laishram Ranjit. People in the area say he had laid down his arms before the government in July along with 46 other cadres.

Local people do not accept the claim of a gunfight. A woman neighbour said there was no encounter: first there was a sound of knocking on the door, and then one or two shots were fired. They allege that Ranjit was killed in custody.

The general secretary of the Yurembam Awang Leikai Apunba Meira Paibi asked why Manipur Police were not seen in the operation. She said suspects should be arrested and tried according to the law, not killed.
nazar: In Manipur, the women of the Meira Paibi have stood in the front line against excesses by security forces for decades. The question raised by the death of a man who had already surrendered is serious, and only an independent judicial inquiry can answer it, not a police statement.
sawal: Ranjit had laid down his arms. What did he have to shoot with?
ref: Meira Paibi
A traditional movement of Manipur's women, who keep watch over neighbourhoods carrying torches and have long fought against drugs and excesses by security forces.
KCP
Kangleipak Communist Party, a banned militant group in Manipur with several factions.

h: Students begin indefinite sit-in in Srinagar over recruitment scam
dek: Former MP Aga Ruhullah joined students sitting in Sher-e-Kashmir Park against alleged rigging in JKSSB exams.
ask: Postpone JKSSB exams until the inquiry is complete
body: Students are on an indefinite sit-in at Srinagar's Sher-e-Kashmir Park against alleged irregularities in recruitment exams held by the Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB). On Saturday, former Lok Sabha MP Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi joined them and said he had come to stand with them, not to lead them.

The demand is that upcoming exams be put off until the allegations of cheating and paper leaks are fully investigated and those responsible are punished. Recently, during an exam in Jammu, the police caught an alleged high-tech cheating gang, and 14 people, including four government employees, were arrested. A special investigation team is looking into the whole network.

One student at the sit-in recalled that three exams were also cancelled in 2022 and 2023 because of irregularities. Ruhullah held both the Lieutenant Governor's administration and the elected government responsible and demanded accountability from senior officials.

PDP president Mehbooba Mufti and Mirwaiz Umar Farooq also called for an inquiry. The report quoted minister Shamima Firdous as saying that if irregularities in the Finance Accounts Assistant exam were proven, strict action would follow, and that an inquiry had been ordered.
nazar: For unemployed young people in Kashmir, a government job is almost the only way forward. Exams cancelled every few months are eating up both their age and their trust. If accountability is not fixed all the way to the top, this anger will go beyond the streets.
sawal: How did the cheating gang keep running even after three exams were cancelled?
ref: JKSSB
Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board, which recruits for lower-level government jobs in the union territory.
SIT
Special Investigation Team, a police team set up to investigate a particular case.

h: Anganwadi workers rally in Jagdalpur, demand regular jobs
dek: After a three-day strike, anganwadi workers in Bastar handed a memorandum to the collector.
ask: Regular jobs or a monthly honorarium of Rs 30,000
body: In Jagdalpur in Bastar district, anganwadi workers and helpers took out a rally after a three-day strike and handed a memorandum to the district collector on 20 November.

Their demands are clear: either their jobs should be made regular, or they should be paid an honorarium of Rs 30,000 a month. All workers should have a path to promotion as supervisors, and workers and helpers should get benefits on retirement. Union leader Khembati Nag put this amount at Rs 10 lakh.

On the same day in Shimla, Himachal Pradesh, outsourced government employees also protested under the leadership of CITU. Leaders there said that the Rs 1,000 rise in the honorarium of anganwadi workers and helpers, which was to take effect from April, came into force only from November, meaning seven months of arrears were lost. The Rs 25 a day rise in the minimum wage announced in the budget has also not yet been notified.
In both places, the workers warned that the agitation would grow if the government did not act.
nazar: Anganwadi centres are the first link for children's nutrition and mothers' health, and in an Adivasi (indigenous) region like Bastar, often the only link. Keeping the women who run them on an 'honorarium' for years and sending them home empty-handed in old age exposes the government's priorities.
sawal: What does a woman who runs an anganwadi centre in Bastar get when she retires?
ref: Anganwadi
A village or neighbourhood centre under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), where young children and pregnant women get nutrition and care.
CITU
Centre of Indian Trade Unions, one of the country's big workers' organisations.

h: Don't fill our pond for a coal mine road, say people of Githauri
dek: Villagers have been sitting on the embankment for three days over the alleged filling of the village's fifty-year-old pond to build a road to a mine.
ask: Stop filling the pond at once
body: In Githauri village in the Ghunghuti area, on the border of Shahdol district, women, men and young people have been sitting in protest on the embankment of the village pond for three days. The village of about 250 people alleges that Bajrang Power company is dumping earth into part of the pond to fill it and build a road to its coal mine.

According to the villagers, the pond is more than fifty years old and it is their only source of water. Their daily needs and their cattle's thirst are met from it, and there are fields all around it.

The villagers also allege that the company is taking over grazing land and that trees are being cut in the forest for the mine. During the protest there was also a scuffle between villagers and company staff, after which people went to the Ghunghuti police outpost and demanded that the work be stopped.

According to the outpost in-charge, a meeting between company officials and villagers has already been held. The company says it has government permission to run the mine. The villagers are asking whether that permission also covers filling in their only source of water.
nazar: In Madhya Pradesh's coal belt, every new mine road runs over some village's shared resource: a pond, a grazing ground, a forest. Permission to mine cannot mean licence to take away a village's water. The administration should stop the work and order an inquiry on the spot.
sawal: Where does the mining permission mention Githauri's pond?
ref: Nistar pond
A village's shared pond, on which everyone has a traditional right. In Madhya Pradesh such water sources are recorded separately in revenue records.
Grazing land
The shared village land left open for grazing cattle.

h: Kanar's village head on hunger strike for ten days, village firm on road demand
dek: People of Kanar village in Pithoragarh held a sit-in outside the DM's office for the Baram-Kanar road, while the village head is on a fast unto death.
body: People of Kanar village in Uttarakhand's Pithoragarh district are standing firm on their demand for the Baram-Kanar road. On Saturday, the fast unto death of village head Sarita Devi entered its tenth day.

In the morning, the villagers held a sit-in for about an hour and a half outside the District Magistrate's office and said the agitation would go on until concrete action was taken. Sarita Devi also sat in the protest and said plainly that she would not end her fast until the demand was met.
In the afternoon, a team from the administration told her that her blood pressure was low, but she still refused to end her fast.

Senior forest department officials also reached the Kanar area. According to the report, they listed the difficulties posed by wildlife sanctuary rules, while the villagers say the matter has been hanging for years and they have received assurances from the very top. Ganesh Prasad, head of Kauli-Kanyal, a district panchayat member and several other local representatives have also joined the agitation.
nazar: For remote mountain villages, a road is the condition for reaching a hospital, a school and a market. Finding a way between sanctuary rules and a village's needs is the government's job. It should not take a woman village head going hungry for ten days.
sawal: After ten days of fasting, where is the road file stuck?
ref: Fast unto death
An open-ended hunger strike until a demand is met, in which protesters say they are ready to stake their lives.
Wildlife sanctuary
A protected area for wildlife, where building anything like a road needs approval from the wildlife board.

h: Hunger for gold, poison of mercury: the Munduruku's rivers are sick
dek: Al Jazeera's 'Fault Lines' film shows how mercury from illegal mining in the Amazon has reached the plates of an Indigenous people.
body: The lives of the Munduruku people of Brazil's Amazon forest revolve around the river and fish. Fish is their daily food, part of both their kitchen and their culture. This new film from Al Jazeera's investigative programme 'Fault Lines' begins with that fish, which has now been poisoned with mercury.

According to the film, the root of this lies in the rising price of gold. The more expensive gold gets on the world market, the deeper illegal miners push into the forest. These miners use mercury to separate gold from soil and sand. The mercury flows into the rivers, builds up in the bodies of fish and then reaches the people who live on those same fish.

Al Jazeera senior correspondent Josh Rushing goes among Indigenous families who are suffering the health damage of this mining while also fighting to save their land. A key part of the film is Rushing getting right inside an illegal mine, where cameras usually cannot go, and seeing how mercury is used to extract gold.

The film also features a researcher who is recording the spread of this poison through Indigenous settlements, and a federal prosecutor who is trying to stop the mercury trade. So the story is not only about the victims, but also about the whole machinery working to measure and stop this harm.

The film also asks why illegal mining does not stop despite government action. It answers by pointing to the market: as long as world demand for gold and its price stay high, there will be profit for miners in the forest.

For background, the Munduruku live in the Tapajós river region of Pará, a state in northern Brazil, and in recent years have kept raising their voices against illegal mining on their land. In the end, this twenty-five-minute film leaves the basic question that lies at its heart: who is paying the real price of the gold that goes into the world's jewellery and vaults?
nazar: This story is from the Amazon, but it is not unfamiliar to us. In the Adivasi (indigenous) areas of Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand, the burden of mining falls on those whose land holds the minerals, while the profit goes elsewhere. Poisoned rivers, sick bodies and a long fight for compensation are all familiar here too.
India is among the world's biggest buyers of gold. So the question is for us too: through which forest and which river has the gold in our weddings and savings come?
sawal: If mercury gets into the fish, what will the children of the Tapajós eat?
ref: Munduruku
An Indigenous people of Brazil's Amazon region who live mainly in the Tapajós river basin. They are known for their struggle against illegal mining and dams on their land.
Mercury and gold mining
In small-scale and illegal mining, mercury is used to bind gold particles. Once in a river it turns into methylmercury, which harms the human body and brain through fish.

h: Forgiveness is not a deal: a hard question, with Derrida's help
dek: In her essay, Gargi Mishra draws on Jacques Derrida's ideas to ask whom forgiveness heals, and whether crimes like genocide or colonial violence can ever be forgiven.
body: Gargi Mishra, who has a PhD in sociology and works in poetry, translation and feature writing, published this essay in the 'Samkaleen' (contemporary) section of Sammukh. It opens with a personal question: is forgiving a cure for the soul, or a quiet prayer to keep oneself going? According to the writer, forgiveness often serves the one who forgives more than the one who did wrong, because it is a release from the bitterness built up inside.

Then the essay turns to the French philosopher Jacques Derrida (1930-2004), who wrote on ethics and politics in his last years. Derrida argued that true forgiveness is unconditional. If it rests on an apology, remorse or reform, it is not forgiveness but a transaction.

The writer sets out the two ends Derrida described: on one side, unconditional ethical forgiveness; on the other, political reconciliation that happens within power, compromise and institutions. Each needs the other, but institutional forgiveness soon becomes a strategy. She tests South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, Rwanda's gacaca courts, Germany's apology to the Jews after the Second World War and the symbolic apologies of Canada and Australia to their native peoples against this measure.

The sharpest question is this: who will forgive on behalf of those who were killed? Can a nation forgive a crime it did not itself suffer? According to the writer, even after Germany's reparations many survivors refused to forgive, and that refusal shows that forgiveness cannot be imposed.

Coming to the present, she talks about 'cancel culture', public shaming and apologies written for PR, where an apology has become a performance. Her conclusion is that forgiveness is neither forgetting nor making excuses, but a new relationship with memory, one that keeps the wound alive without becoming its prisoner.
nazar: In India, after riots, caste massacres and custodial deaths, it is often the victims who are expected to 'move on' and 'forget', while no apology is made and no justice is done. This essay reminds us that if the pressure to reconcile is placed on the weak, it is not forgiveness but enforced silence. From 1984 to Gujarat and Manipur, the question is the one the writer raises: who has the right to forgive on behalf of the dead?
sawal: Who is expected to reconcile when no one has apologised?
ref: Jacques Derrida
French philosopher (1930-2004), father of the theory of 'deconstruction'. In his last years he wrote on hospitality, forgiveness and justice.
Truth and Reconciliation Commission
A commission set up in South Africa after the end of apartheid, where those who confessed their crimes were offered a path to amnesty. Critics see it as forgiveness with conditions.
photo_note: A gathering of poets and Sufis

h: The 'good woman' badge and the lives buried beneath it
dek: In the seventh part of her series on marriage, Pallavi Vinod shows how praise for the 'good woman' has, for generations, extracted the price of women's unpaid labour and self-erasure.
body: Fiction writer Pallavi Vinod is writing a series of essays on marriage and family life on Sammukh called 'Dampatya' (married life). The argument of the seventh part, 'Achchhi Auratein' (Good Women), is simple: the 'good woman' label has really been a tool to extract unpaid work and sacrifice from women, and their suffering lies buried in the foundations of civilisation.

The writer remembers the girls married off as children into strangers' homes, who were expected to forget their parents' home and whose reward was two meals a day. Bearing eight or ten children was called 'good fortune', and dying a married woman was the highest honour. The 'bad woman', by contrast, was one who ate first, saved her own children's share or refused to toil more than was needed.

The story of an aunt brings this difference to life: she read novels while cooking, spoke openly about her husband's straying and left a fifteen-room ancestral house for a two-room flat. Her children did well, yet relatives kept cursing her. Even in nuclear families, praise went to the woman who never asked for help, and the husband who shared the work was mocked.

On the state of working women, the writer gives the example of a friend named Surekha, whose joy at getting a job turned into exhaustion after marriage under countless household chores and the burden of loans. Even women officers in high posts are expected to cover their heads at home. The writer says a poster in a doctor's clinic stated that about three-quarters of rheumatoid arthritis patients in India are women, and she asks whether this is the result of generations of neglecting their own bodies.
The essay's final message is that women should become not 'good women' but 'good human beings'. Raising children, relationships and care are a shared responsibility, not only a woman's duty.
nazar: Time use surveys show again and again that Indian women spend many times more hours than men on unpaid household work, yet this labour counts neither in GDP nor in the family's honour. This essay catches the moral language that turns this unpaid labour into sacred 'sacrifice'. Until the definition of the 'good daughter-in-law' changes, even the growing number of working women will not bring equality.
sawal: When the aunt read novels, what was it that annoyed the relatives?
ref: Kalighat painting
A style of the patua artists around Kolkata's Kalighat temple in the nineteenth century, which also carries sharp satire on babu culture and domestic relationships.
Unpaid domestic work
Labour like cooking, cleaning and caring for children and the elderly, most of which is done by women and which is not recorded in economic statistics.
photo_note: Kalighat painting: a woman holding a broom

h: Zweig's 'Beware of Pity': the pity that runs from pain
dek: Rereading Stefan Zweig's only novel, fiction writer and Zweig translator Oma Sharma says the difference between sentimental pity and true compassion is the axis of the book.
body: Oma Sharma, born in Bulandshahr and living in Mumbai, has translated Zweig's autobiography and stories into Hindi. In this piece in Samalochan, he begins with Italo Calvino's idea that a classic is a book that gives something new on every reading. According to him, Zweig's 1939 novel is just such a book.

The story is set in 1914. Anton Hofmiller, a lieutenant at a cavalry garrison near Vienna, goes to a party at the home of the wealthy Kekesfalva family and unknowingly asks their seventeen-year-old daughter Edith, who is paralysed, to dance. Embarrassment takes him back to that house again and again. Edith falls in love with him, but Anton, caught between pity and fear of the shame of 'buying a rich bride', can neither refuse her nor accept her. In the end war breaks out, his letter saying yes never arrives, and Edith takes her own life.

At the centre of Sharma's piece is the difference between two kinds of pity. One is sentimental pity, which is really the giver's attempt to escape his own unease. The other is the patient compassion of Dr Condor, which stays with the sufferer and demands sacrifice. Condor's idea that no illness is incurable forever, only for now, is also important in the piece.

The writer also reads the novel politically. Zweig wrote it in 1938 while in exile in England, as Nazism and fascism were rising in Europe. In the story of Edith's father, Sharma sees the fragility of European Jewish life and bourgeois wealth. Finally he compares it with Thomas Mann's 'The Magic Mountain' and Camus's 'The Plague', where Camus's characters resist and Zweig's withdraw into themselves.
nazar: Here, disability is still mostly seen through the lens of pity, not of rights and equality. Zweig's novel, and Sharma's reading of it, show how cruel a pity that looks generous on the surface can be. And a book written in exile amid the rise of fascism also reminds us that the failure of personal relationships is often the shadow of a larger political darkness.
sawal: The letter that never reached Edith: whose failure was it, Anton's or the times'?
ref: Stefan Zweig
Austrian Jewish writer (1881-1942) who fled the Nazis to England and then to Brazil. 'The World of Yesterday' is his famous autobiography.
Beware of Pity
Zweig's only complete novel (1939); its original German title is 'Ungeduld des Herzens'.
photo_note: A woman writing a love letter

h: Why is going to Delhi to study called 'awaragardi'?
dek: Uzma Kalam's new story is about Shaheen, a small-town girl who has won admission to a central university in Delhi and must fight her family for her right to study.
body: According to the introduction by Janaki Pul's moderator, Uzma Kalam has made a distinct name as a fiction writer in a short time and writes about the tangles of lower-middle-class life in a traditional storytelling style. Her story collection 'Kaali Billiyon Ke Saaye Mein Chatori Chudail' (A Greedy Witch in the Shadow of Black Cats) is already out. 'Awaragardi' (Loafing About) is her new story.

The story is about Shaheen, daughter of a lower-middle-class Muslim family in a small town in north India. The only sister of three brothers, Shaheen has won admission to a central university in Delhi, where fees are low, and she wants to cover her hostel costs by giving tuition. But the document check and fee deadlines are close, and her family still has to be won over.

It begins with an innocent bargain made with God during the Maghrib (evening) prayer. Then comes Ammi's fear of what will happen to the family's honour if an unmarried daughter lives away from home, and Abba's worried silence, which usually gives in to his wife. Ammi holds up the example of cousin Rabia, who was obedient and was married into a rich family, and Shaheen hits back with sarcasm and witty replies.

Shaheen goes on a hunger strike, which the family takes lightly, and finally announces that she will leave home. The parents give way, caught between fear of disgrace and fear of losing their daughter, and a ticket for 19 May is booked. Just then her maternal uncle, aunt and grandmother turn up, and the cries about honour begin. The story's most important turn is that this time Ammi herself stands up for her daughter.

The story tells serious questions with humour and satire: the policing of women's movement, treating marriage as the measure of a daughter's worth, and watching over girls with words like 'awaragardi'. The full story can be read on Janaki Pul.
nazar: Enrolment of Muslim girls in higher education has risen in recent years, but behind every admission lie many such battles inside the home that do not show in the figures. This story records them, without making religion the villain. That is why the low fees and hostels of central universities are a door to freedom for a poor family's daughter, and making them expensive would shut that door.
sawal: If the fees had been higher, could Shaheen's fight have even begun?
ref: Janaki Pul
A Hindi literary web magazine started around 2010, moderated by writer Prabhat Ranjan. It publishes stories, poems, reviews and translations.
Central university
Universities set up by an Act of Parliament and funded by the central government, such as Jamia, JNU and Delhi University, where fees are usually low.

h: When Ram returned, who cleaned Ayodhya?
dek: In an excerpt from a collection of ten new Ramayana stories, published in Scroll, Nishit Jain sees Ram's coronation through the eyes of the palace washerman and sweeper.
body: The collection 'Our Ramayanas: The Epic Retold in Ten New Stories', published by HarperCollins India, brings together stories by ten new writers that retell the epic through the eyes of less familiar characters. The introduction and illustrations are by Devdutt Pattanaik. Scroll has published an excerpt from Nishit Jain's story 'The City Cleaners'.

After fourteen years of exile, Ayodhya is glittering in preparation for the return of Ram, Sita and Lakshman, courtyards are being washed and lamps set out. But the story does not follow the royal family. Its heroes are the palace washerman Shuddhak and the sweeper Bhring, and their wives Nirvani and Prashni, who watch everything from the rooftop and the river ghat. Shuddhak's complaint is very practical: who will clean up after the army of monkeys, and a celebration does not raise wages.

At the Sarayu ghat the difference becomes sharper. Priests fill pots while chanting the names of the seven sacred rivers, and Shuddhak, beating clothes on a stone, says their water is holy and his is dirty. On coronation day the sweepers are pushed to the edge of the courtyard, close enough to see, far enough that their shadow does not fall on the sacred water. Vasishtha anoints Ram and Vishwamitra prays that dharma may prevail over 'matsya nyaya'.

In the women's quarters, whispers begin when they see the mark of Ravan's grip on Sita's arm. For a reader who knows the Ram story, this hint is heavy, because later it is a washerman's words that become the pretext for Sita's exile. The excerpt ends with Prashni saying that dharma never stops at their doorstep.
nazar: The Ayodhya that has today been made a symbol of grandeur and displays of faith is seen in this story through the eyes of those whose labour makes every celebration possible and who are pushed to the side every time. The story never uses the word 'caste', but it is present everywhere in its talk of purity, shadows and wages. Cleaning work still falls mostly to Dalit communities, and deaths in sewers have not stopped.
sawal: What threat did Shuddhak's shadow pose to the sacred water?
ref: Matsya nyaya
A concept in ancient Indian political thought, meaning the 'law of the fish': a chaos in which the big fish swallows the small. Preventing it was seen as the job of the state.
The washerman episode
A story from the Uttarakanda in which, after a washerman's taunt, Ram sends the pregnant Sita to the forest. The episode often comes up in debates on a king's duty and injustice to women.
photo_note: Ram, Sita and Lakshman returning to Ayodhya

h: 'Amarkeet': the worm of fear and a neighbourhood's silent consent
dek: Vijayshankar Chaturvedi's new story shows, through the eyes of a retired clerk, how manufactured fear turns a neighbourhood obedient and makes people watch over one another.
body: Born in 1970 in Aama village in Satna district, Vijayshankar Chaturvedi is a poet, fiction writer and a journalist of more than three decades, and was part of Jansatta's Mumbai team. His novel 'Vidushak' (The Jester) was serialised in Jansatta in the nineties, and his book on human judgement in the age of AI and algorithms, 'Nirnay Ka Sthapatya' (The Architecture of Decision), came out in September 2026. 'Amarkeet' is his new story on Sammukh.

At the heart of the story is Bilveshwar Sharma, a mid-level officer retired from the revenue department, whose honesty meant there was never much money at home, which is why his wife Javitri Devi is always cross. One morning the newspaper carries two sensational reports, and an astrologer announces that behind the septic tanks bursting in the city is an immortal worm, the 'Amarkeet' (deathless worm), recorded in some ancient text.

After this, fear spreads through the whole lane. His son Sucharu falls ill, a black line is seen creeping across floors and lanes, and neighbours like Mishra, Gupta and Rahman start keeping a closer watch on one another than on their own homes. Government announcements on TV bring a compulsory 'process' and white packets bearing a familiar face, and those who refuse are called a danger to everyone. Sharma hesitates; the others quickly agree.

In the end the lane is orderly and silent, and the son is calm and obedient, as if he feels nothing at all. Sharma understands that now it is those who resist who are the 'danger', and that the neighbourhood has begun to police itself. The story ends with his illness and the realisation that he himself has become a burden. The full story can be read on Sammukh.
nazar: This allegory names no country or leader, but the manufactured panic, the orders coming from the TV and the 'face on the packet' remind the reader of many familiar things. The most frightening part is that in the end no police are needed; neighbours become watchers of neighbours. This is the greatest danger to a democracy: when a citizen who disagrees starts being called 'a danger to everyone'.
sawal: In the story, whose face is printed on the white packet?
ref: Allegory
A story in which events and characters stand as symbols of a larger social or political truth, like Orwell's 'Animal Farm'.
Gaganendranath Tagore
Bengali painter and cartoonist (1867-1938). In series like 'Virup Vajra' he struck hard at religious hypocrisy and babu culture.
